newsitem.title: INDIA: India to import wheat for first time in four years.
newsitem.headline: India to import wheat for first time in four years.

text.p: India on Thursday became a net wheat importer when it decided to import two million tonnes of wheat in the current financial year to augment domestic supplies and check rising prices.
Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav said India will import two million tonnes of wheat in fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) to meet the shortfall.

"The government has decided during the current financial year it will import two million tonnes of wheat," Yadav told the Indian parliament at the end of a debate on the rising prices of essential commodities.
India last imported two million tonnes of wheat in 1991/92. It exported 600,000 tonnes in 1995/96 and 1.07 million tonnes up to September 30 this year, when the government halted exports.
It was not immediately clear whether the government would import throught the state-owned agencies or allow the private traders to import.

Prem Garg, a leading Delhi foodgrains exporter, told Reuters wheat in the domestic markets was currently priced at around 6,700 rupees per tonne but it would soon fall below 6,000 rupees on news of wheat imports.
"The prices will fall by at least 20-25 percent on the news of wheat imports," Garg said.
Some analysts said earlier that growers were holding back stocks in order to drive prices up further, and later sell to the government at a larger profit.
"India will be mainly looking towards Australia and Argentina for its wheat imports," Garg said.
Traders said on Wednesday that dwindling government reserves had caused wheat prices to rise sharply in recent months compared with prices last year.
Earlier analysts had said that even without imports, domestic prices should start to fall in February since the new crop was due in March.
India expects a wheat crop of about 64 million tonnes in 1997. A clear picture should emerge by early February.
Government wheat procurement in the 1995/96 growing season fell to 8.2 million tonnes from 12.3 million the previous year due to a three-million-tonne shortfall in output.
As of October 1, the state-run Food Corporation of India held 19.6 million tonnes of foodgrain -- wheat, rice and other cereals -- down from 29.9 million a year earlier.
But October stocks were well above the buffer norm set by the government of 16.6 million tonnes.
Foodgrain stocks have fallen steadily from 25.27 million tonnes in July, down from 32.01 million tonnes in August 1995.
